_doc: What every monster family is weak to, resists and shrugs off, and what its nature refuses or falls to easily, decided from its LORE (winning-build plan 2026-11-13 section 3.2; Brandon: 'lore, not floor'). tools/content/affinity_pass.py --write writes it into data/monsters.json (`weaknesses`, `resistances`, `shrugs_off`, `status_immune`, `status_weak`); data/affinity_rules.json holds the steps (weak x2, resisted x0.5, shrugs off x0.25, cap x3). tests/test_affinity_lore.py checks every family has a profile with a lore note and a source, that monsters.json matches this file, and that every lock has a key above it.

_schema.layers: A kind's profile is its family's, then its group's (if it is in one), then its own (kinds), then the tag rules. FORM (slash, pierce, blunt) comes wholly from the layers: each layer may set a form to weak, resist, shrugs_off or neutral, later layers winning. A named foe (boss, mini-boss, seal demon) keeps the forms written on it in monsters.json unless `kinds` names its form. ELEMENTS and SUBSTANCES (fire, holy, silver, iron...) start from the kind's own lists in monsters.json: a family or tag rule adds softly (never against the kind's own opposite word), a group or kind adds by force (it moves the type from the opposite list); `drop` removes a type from all three lists. STATUS lists: a group's or kind's list, when given, replaces its family's; the tag rules then add to status_immune and take what is immune out of status_weak.
_schema.status_immune: the effect never takes hold, and the game says why (Monster.add_effect, affinity.status_line)
_schema.status_weak: it takes hold without a big foe's resist roll and lasts half again as long; the token fear_of_fire means a fire hit puts it to flight (not on a kind that resists fire, nor on a named foe, who is never routed)
_schema.holy: holy weakness is for the unholy only: the tags in unholy.tags, and the cursed kinds named in unholy.cursed. Every other kind loses holy from its weaknesses.

unholy.lore: Holy power burns whatever has turned against heaven, be it the dead who will not lie down, the fiends of the pit or those few whose very nature is a curse, but against an honest bear a blessed blade is no more than any other blade.
unholy.source: The Christian rite of exorcism (holy water and the sign of the cross against demons and the restless dead); the plan's ruling, section 3.2: 'Holy is narrowed to the unholy (undead, demons, the cursed)'.

cursed.werewolf: Lycaon served Zeus human flesh and was turned into a wolf for it: lycanthropy is a curse.
cursed.werewolf_alpha: Sigmund and Sinfjotli put on cursed wolf skins and could not take them off for ten days.
cursed.elder_werewolf: The oldest of the cursed: the wolf has long since eaten the man.
cursed.wererat: A cursed man, as every were-beast is.
cursed.weretiger: The harimau jadian is a man cursed to become a tiger after dark.
cursed.corrupted_angel: One of the third of the stars the dragon's tail swept from heaven (Revelation 12:4): fallen.
cursed.pegasus_corrupted: A creature of heaven turned rotten: holy light burns what it fell from.
cursed.unicorn_corrupted: The unicorn's horn cleansed poisoned pools; this one's horn poisons them.
cursed.nothic: The curse that answers a wizard's greed bent him into this shape.
cursed.ker: The Keres are the death-spirits of the battlefield, gorging on the blood of the fallen (Hesiod, Shield of Heracles).
cursed.lamia: Grief and Hera's curse turned a queen into a devourer of children.
cursed.bone_golem: A necromancer built it from the bones of the dead and bound it with death-magic.
cursed.gnoll_fang_of_yeenoghu: Marked by the demon lord Yeenoghu: his taint runs in its blood.
cursed.gnoll_alpha_of_yeenoghu: It ate the demon-tainted flesh of the alpha before it.
cursed.mere_wife: The Beowulf poet names Grendel's kin the race of Cain, whom the Creator outlawed and condemned.
cursed.kallikantzaros: The kallikantzaroi flee the blessing of the waters at Epiphany: holy water drives them back under the earth.
cursed.image_of_the_beast: Made to be worshipped in the Beast's place (Revelation 13): an idol, and a cursed thing.
cursed.redcap: Border folk drove him off with words of Scripture or the sight of a cross (the folklore of the Scottish Border).
cursed.shadow_assassin: He bartered away his own shadow for the right to walk in shadows, and holy light finds him out.
cursed.shadow_archer: He learned his craft from the darkness and fletches his arrows with it, so holy light burns him.

undead.lore: The dead know no sleep, and poison finds no living blood to ride. They have no affection that a charm might win (a hero with the Helm of Aragorn's oath is the one exception: Monster.resists_control).
undead.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the undead are immune to sleep, charm and poison.

demon.lore: Whatever fiend comes up out of the pit, holy power will burn it.
demon.source: The rite of exorcism; Revelation 20 (the devil cast into the lake of fire).

construct.lore: That which was made has no mind to frighten, muddle or charm, and it never sleeps, nor has it any blood for poison to work in.
construct.source: The golem of Prague (Rabbi Judah Loew's clay servant) obeys the word on its brow and nothing else.

plant.lore: A plant has no mind that could be frightened, charmed or confused, and it has no eyes to be blinded.
plant.source: Natural history; the old rule of Monster.resists_control, now written down.

elemental.lore: Fire, stone, wind and water that have come to life can neither be put to sleep nor poisoned.
elemental.source: Paracelsus, A Book on Nymphs, Sylphs, Pygmies and Salamanders (1566): the elemental beings are made of their element alone.

fey.lore: Iron has ever been the bane of fairies, and so mothers laid an iron knife in the cradle or hung a horseshoe over the door to keep them off.
fey.source: British and Irish folk belief, recorded by W. B. Yeats, Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888), and Katharine Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies (1976).

restless_dead.lore: The walking dead have no blood to lose and no heart to stop, so that a thrust finds nothing to kill, and the old way with them is to cut off the head.
restless_dead.source: Grettis saga, ch. 35: Grettir wrestles the draugr Glámr, cuts off his head and burns the body.

ghosts.lore: A ghost parts like mist before the blade, so that every common blow is all but wasted upon it, and it is holy power and fire that lay it to rest.
ghosts.source: Shakespeare, Hamlet 1.1: the Ghost 'is, as the air, invulnerable, and our vain blows malicious mockery.'

vampires_liches.lore: In the old tales a vampire is slain with a stake through the heart, and so a thrust is the way to kill one.
vampires_liches.source: Bram Stoker, Dracula (1897), ch. 16: Arthur drives the stake through Lucy's heart.

demons.lore: The fiends of the pit wear flesh as men wear a coat, and blades bite it as they bite any other, but it is holy power and cold iron that truly hurt them.
demons.source: Medieval exorcism manuals (holy water); cold iron against spirits in British folk belief (Katharine Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies).

dragons.lore: The scales of a dragon turn the sword's edge, but a thrust finds the gap, as Bard's black arrow found the bare patch on Smaug's breast and as Sigurd stabbed Fafnir from below. Dragons breathe fire and cannot be burned by it, and they sleep deeply upon their gold.
dragons.source: Volsunga saga, ch. 18 (Sigurd in the pit); Tolkien, The Hobbit (1937), ch. 14 (the black arrow); Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4: Medea sings the sleepless dragon of the Golden Fleece to sleep.

giants.lore: Giants are mighty but slow of wit and easily confused, and many a tale tells how some small hero tricked them into fighting one another.
giants.source: Jack the Giant Killer (English fairy tale): Jack throws stones at two sleeping giants until each thinks the other struck him; Odyssey 9: 'Nobody' blinds the Cyclops.

goblinkin.lore: Goblins, orcs, kobolds and gnolls are flesh and leather as men are, and no secret lore or key is needed to slay them. Their strength is in their numbers and their war-bands.
goblinkin.source: Tolkien, The Hobbit (1937): the goblins of the Misty Mountains fall to plain swords (Orcrist and Glamdring) like any foe.

mortals.lore: Men and women are hurt by whatever would hurt any of us, and nothing but the armour upon their backs will change the blow.
mortals.source: Common sense, and every war ever fought.

fair_folk.lore: The fair folk have ever feared iron, for though they are clever and quick and an ordinary blade cuts them as it cuts other folk, iron burns them.
fair_folk.source: Yeats, Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry (1888); Briggs, A Dictionary of Fairies (1976).

great_beasts.lore: Wolves, bears, lions and boars are but flesh and fur, and since every beast fears fire a torch will keep the pack at bay.
great_beasts.source: Kipling, The Jungle Book (1894), 'Mowgli's Brothers': Mowgli drives off Shere Khan and the wolves with the Red Flower, fire.

vermin.lore: Rats, bats, beetles and spiders are so small that the right blow ends them: a beetle's shell turns an edge but cracks beneath a boot, and a blade hardly touches a swarm.
vermin.source: Natural history (an insect's armour is its outer shell); the Pied Piper of Hamelin, for the rats' weakness for a tune.

serpents.lore: Snakes, lizards and frogs are flesh and scale, and the old charmers know a tune to which the cobra will sway.
serpents.source: Psalm 58:4-5 ('the deaf adder ... which will not hearken to the voice of charmers'); the snake charmers of India and Egypt.

birds.lore: Birds are so light and hollow of bone that an arrow brings them down.
birds.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.6: Heracles scares the Stymphalian birds up with a bronze rattle and shoots them down.

gorgons.lore: Gorgons and basilisks kill with a look, and therefore Perseus beheld only the reflection of Medusa when he took her head with a curved sword.
gorgons.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4; Pliny, Natural History 8.33 (the basilisk).

legend.lore: The monsters of the old stories fell each in its own fashion, and the weakness of each lies in its story: see the kinds.
legend.source: Apollodorus, Library (the Labours of Heracles); Hesiod, Theogony.

shapeshifters.lore: The body of a shapeshifter is not wholly real, so that its wounds close almost as fast as they are made, but to its curse there is a key.
shapeshifters.source: European folk belief about the were-beasts (see the werewolves group).

constructs.lore: Things of bronze, iron, clay and stone turn the blade, which skates off them or sticks fast, but a hammer cracks them.
constructs.source: The golem of Prague (clay) and Hephaestus's bronze Talos (Apollonius, Argonautica 4); a smith's sense of metal and stone.

elementals.lore: Living fire, air and water close behind the blade as if no wound had been given, and living stone turns it aside, but the hammer and the opposing element will break them.
elementals.source: Paracelsus, A Book on Nymphs, Sylphs, Pygmies and Salamanders (1566); the Sumerian poem Lugal-e (Ninurta's mace Sharur breaks the stone army of Asag).

oozes.lore: A jelly closes about a thrust and does but tremble at a blow, so that only an edge, cold or fire truly harms it, and some jellies split when they are cut.
oozes.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the gelatinous cube, the black pudding (cutting divides it) and the oozes; they are blind and mindless.

aberrations.lore: Aberrations come from outside the world, and each was made wrong in its own fashion: see the kinds.
aberrations.source: Lovecraft's star-spawn and the Dungeons & Dragons aberrations (the beholder, the mind flayer, the mimic).

plants.lore: An arrow sticks idly in the trunk of a tree, but an axe will fell it and fire will take it, for dry wood kindles very readily.
plants.source: The woodsman's trade; Tolkien gives the Ents the same dread of axe and fire (The Two Towers, 1954).

celestials.lore: The children of heaven have no dread of holy power, but they fear shadow and the magic of death.
celestials.source: Revelation; Dionysius the Areopagite, The Celestial Hierarchy.

skeletons.lore: Bare bones snap beneath a mace, while a blade slides away from them and a thrust passes between the ribs and finds nothing.
skeletons.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): 'sharp and/or edged weapons do only half damage to skeletons; blunt weapons do normal damage.'

armoured.lore: Plate turns the edge of a sword and most points besides, and it was for men in plate that the mace and the war hammer were made.
armoured.source: Medieval arms: the flanged mace and the war hammer spread across Europe with plate armour in the fourteenth century.

shades.lore: These dead have no body at all, being made only of cold and shadow, and every ordinary blow passes straight through them.
shades.source: Homer, Odyssey 11: three times Odysseus tried to embrace his mother's shade, and three times she slipped from his arms like a shadow or a dream.

liches.lore: A lich has set its death outside its body, so that blade and point do it little harm, though its bones may still be broken.
liches.source: The Russian tale of Koschei the Deathless (Afanasyev): his death is hidden in a needle, in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a chest under an oak.

devils.lore: The devils of the deeper pits fear silver, as witches do, because it is the pure metal.
devils.source: English and German folk belief: silver drives off the Devil and witches (the silver bullet or the silver sixpence); Dungeons & Dragons gives the devils the same weakness.

mimics.lore: The skin of a mimic sweats a glue stronger than pitch, so that a club or a mace sticks fast and does it little harm.
mimics.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the mimic and its adhesive.

beholders.lore: The beholder's great central eye is its heart and its weakness, and it is undone by a thrust or an arrow into it, or by a blinding.
beholders.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the beholder.

mind_flayers.lore: The masters of the mind can never be muddled or charmed by any lesser mind.
mind_flayers.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the mind flayer.

earth_elementals.lore: Living stone turns every edge and point, but it shatters beneath a hammer.
earth_elementals.source: The Sumerian poem Lugal-e: Ninurta smashes the stone warriors of Asag with his mace Sharur.

fire_elementals.lore: A creature made of fire takes little or no hurt from fire, and a blade passes through the flame of its body, but cold will slay it.
fire_elementals.source: Paracelsus (1566): the salamanders live in fire as fish live in water.

water_elementals.lore: None can cut or stab or crush the water, but lightning and cold go through it.
water_elementals.source: Paracelsus (1566): the undines, the beings of water.

jinn.lore: The jinn were made of smokeless fire, and iron drives them away.
jinn.source: Arab folk belief (the cry 'Hadid! Iron!' against the jinn, recorded by Edward Lane, The Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians, 1836); Qur'an 55:15 (the jinn made of smokeless fire).

jellies.lore: An edge divides a jelly of this kind instead of wounding it worse, and only fire and cold truly harm it.
jellies.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the ochre jelly.

beetles.lore: The shell of a beetle turns an edge, yet it cracks beneath a hammer or a boot.
beetles.source: Natural history: an insect's armour is its hard outer shell, strong against a cut and brittle to a crushing blow.

swarms.lore: A swarm is ten thousand small lives, so that a blade or a point kills two and misses all the rest, and stamping does little better. Fire is the answer to it, as the hot brand is for rot grubs.
swarms.source: Natural history (the locust plagues of Exodus 10); Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): rot grubs are killed by fire on the skin.

trolls.lore: A troll's wounds will close while you watch, unless fire or acid has eaten them, and to be struck by fire also frightens it.
trolls.source: Poul Anderson, Three Hearts and Three Lions (1961): the troll whose severed parts crawl back together until they are burned; Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): fire and acid stop a troll's regeneration.

cyclopes.lore: A one-eyed giant has but one eye to lose, and a thrust is his undoing.
cyclopes.source: Homer, Odyssey 9: Odysseus drives a sharpened olive stake into Polyphemus's eye.

werewolves.lore: Were-beasts heal almost as soon as they are wounded, and only silver and holy power will hurt them properly.
werewolves.source: European folk belief, fixed by the film The Wolf Man (1941): only silver kills the werewolf; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1 (Lycaon cursed into a wolf).

elves.lore: Elves do not slumber as men do, and no magic can put them to sleep.
elves.source: Tolkien's sleepless Elves; Dungeons & Dragons, Player's Handbook (2014): Fey Ancestry ('magic can't put you to sleep').

snakes.lore: A true snake will sway to the charmer's tune, and so it may be charmed out of striking.
snakes.source: Psalm 58:4-5 ('the voice of charmers'); the snake charmers of India.

world_serpents.lore: These are the children of the Midgard Serpent, and Thor's hammer is the blow that kills them.
world_serpents.source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 51: at Ragnarok Thor kills Jormungandr with Mjolnir.

medusas.lore: With one stroke of a curved sword Perseus took the head of Medusa, and a cutting blow is still her undoing.
medusas.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4; Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2 (the harpe Hermes gave Perseus).

hydras.lore: For every head cut from a hydra two grow again, unless the stump is burned.
hydras.source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2: Iolaus sears each stump with a torch as Heracles cuts.

chimeras.lore: Bellerophon thrust a spear tipped with lead into the Chimera's fiery throat, and the fire melted the lead and so slew her.
chimeras.source: John Tzetzes, scholia on Lycophron (the lead-tipped spear); Hesiod, Theogony 319-325.

angels.lore: The soldiers of heaven know no fear, and have no love that a charm might win.
angels.source: Revelation 12:7: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon.

hags.lore: The old hags who sit on the breasts of sleepers know every art of sleep and cannot be lulled.
hags.source: The Old Hag of Newfoundland and the mare of Germanic folklore, who rides the sleeper's chest.

wood_golem.lore: Whatever is made of wood fears a cutting blow, as of the axe, and fears fire.

flesh_golem.lore: It was stitched from the dead, so that a thrust finds no vitals, but a cut will open its seams.

homunculus.lore: The homunculus is a man a foot tall, grown from its maker's blood, and is as small and soft and easy to hurt as a cat.
homunculus.source: Paracelsus, De Natura Rerum (1537): the homunculus grown in a flask.

talos.lore: Talos was all of bronze from head to foot but for a single vein that ran from neck to ankle and was stopped with one bronze nail, and an arrow in the ankle let out his ichor.
talos.source: Apollodorus, Library 1.9.26: Poeas shot Talos in the ankle (or Medea pulled the nail).

bronze_sentinel.lore: This guard was built upon the pattern of Talos and has the flaw of Talos, one point where a thrust gets in.

crystal_ooze.lore: Its jelly has hardened into crystal, which shatters beneath a hammer.

black_pudding.lore: A cutting blow divides a black pudding into two lesser ones, for it does not resist the edge but multiplies beneath it.
black_pudding.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): slashing and lightning split the black pudding.

gas_spore.lore: This puffball drifts in the air full of spores, and one thrust will burst it.
gas_spore.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (1977): the gas spore.

brown_mold.lore: Brown mold drinks up heat, so that fire only feeds it and it can never be set alight.
brown_mold.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Dungeon Masters Guide (1979): brown mold grows from fire.

corrupted_treant.lore: A whole oak has turned to evil, and blows and arrows scarcely mark it, but an axe will fell it yet.
corrupted_treant.source: Tolkien, The Two Towers (1954): the Ents and the axe.

moss_sentinel.lore: The moss is heaped upon a frame of roots and stone, so that a blow sinks into it, but an edge will cut it free.

nemean_lion.lore: No blade or arrow could pierce the hide of the Nemean lion, and so Heracles stunned it with his club and strangled it.

calydonian_boar.lore: Swords glanced from the bristles of the Calydonian boar, until Atalanta's arrow drew first blood and Meleager's spear slew it.

hell_bovine.lore: The cows of the secret level have hides as thick as a barn door, and they care nothing for a club.
hell_bovine.source: Diablo II (2000): the Secret Cow Level.

stymphalian_bird.lore: With a rattle that Athena gave him, Heracles frightened the bronze-feathered birds into the air.

sown_warrior.lore: The Spartoi sprang up from the dragon's teeth, but when Cadmus threw a stone among them each believed that another had struck him, and so in confusion they killed one another.

echidna.lore: Echidna was slain in her sleep by Argus All-Eyes, for sleep is her undoing.

jiangshi.lore: The hopping corpse is stopped dead when a Taoist priest fastens a paper talisman upon its forehead.
jiangshi.source: Chinese folk belief, made famous by the film Mr. Vampire (1985).

grave_guardian.lore: They swore to keep holy ground and were buried standing at the door of the crypt, and the blessing is on them still, so that holy power does not burn them.

undead_colossus.lore: It is a hill of corpses stitched together, and a blow sinks into it, but an axe will hack it apart.

flesh_colossus.lore: This is a hill of stitched flesh, and a blow sinks into it, but an axe will hack it apart.

hrungnirs_ghost.lore: Hrungnir had a heart and a head of stone, and the hammer of Thor shattered both the giant's whetstone and his skull.

mere_wife.lore: Hrunting would not bite on Grendel's mother when Beowulf smote her, and only the giant-forged sword from her own hall could kill her.

cave_troll.lore: The hide of a cave troll is as hard as stone, and a club rebounds from it.
cave_troll.source: Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring (1954): the troll in Moria.

ettin_warchief.lore: Each of his two heads has a thick skull, so that a club does little, but an edge or a point finds a way in.

frostfang_giant.lore: A club rebounds from flesh that is as hard as ice.

sobek_warrior.lore: He wears the hide of a crocodile, which turns a cutting blow.
sobek_warrior.source: Natural history: the crocodile's bony scutes.

mud_crawler.lore: It is armoured in scales that turn a cutting blow.

gibbering_mouther.lore: Its loose flesh is a heap of mouths and eyes, and a blow sinks away into it.
gibbering_mouther.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual II (1983): the gibbering mouther.

lurking_horror.lore: It has no shape of its own, and closes round a thrust.

chaos_spawn.lore: This is a shred of the first Chaos, where an edge or a blow meets nothing that will stay in its place.

girtablilu.lore: The scorpion-men who guard Mashu are armoured as scorpions are: blade and point skate off, but a mace will crack the shell.
girtablilu.source: The Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet IX: the scorpion-men at the mountain gate.

charybdis.lore: The whirlpool has a mouth, and a crushing blow is swallowed by the water.

charybdis_spawn.lore: The whirlpool is little, but it has a mouth, and a crushing blow is swallowed by the water.

the_sphinx.lore: Oedipus overcame the sphinx with an answer, but in the old pictures the heroes go against her with spears.
the_sphinx.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Rex; Greek vase paintings of the sphinx and the spear.

lava_elemental.lore: A hammer does but splash through molten rock, and a point melts in it.

green_knight.lore: Gawain struck off the Green Knight's head with one stroke, and the knight took it up and rode away, for a cutting blow does not trouble him.
green_knight.source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (14th century).

wild_hunt_captain.lore: He rides in the hunt of the sky, and half of him is storm that an edge hardly cuts.

lyssa_madness.lore: Lyssa is madness itself, and so nothing can muddle her.
lyssa_madness.source: Euripides, Heracles: Hera sends Lyssa to drive Heracles mad.

pixie_swarm.lore: These finger-high pranksters fly in a cloud and dodge every blade.
pixie_swarm.source: Devon and Cornwall folk belief (being pixy-led).

khrafstra_swarm.lore: The vermin of the evil spirit seethe in one knot, and blows of every kind do little to it, but fire destroys it.
khrafstra_swarm.source: The Zoroastrian Vendidad: the khrafstra, the noxious creatures.

ice_elemental.lore: An edge or a point skates off living ice, but a hammer will shatter it.
ice_elemental.source: Paracelsus (1566): the elemental beings; the plain physics of ice.

world_serpent.lore: Jormungandr's scales turn blade and point alike, and Thor's hammer is the blow that kills him.

pit_executioner.lore: The headsman of the pit goes clad in a hide of black iron, by which every edge is turned.

risen_deadite.lore: When a deadite rises again its bones are rotten, and a club breaks them apart.
risen_deadite.source: The Evil Dead films (1981-1992): the deadites are hacked and smashed apart.

dahaka_wyrm.lore: Fereydun struck Zahhak down with the ox-headed mace, for a cut or a thrust did but let out the vermin within him.
dahaka_wyrm.source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Fereydun and the ox-headed mace); the Avesta (Azhi Dahaka full of noxious creatures).

tiamat.lore: Marduk drove the winds into the mouth of Tiamat and loosed an arrow that split her belly.

hraesvelg_eagle.lore: The wings of the Corpse-Swallower make all the cold winds of the world, so that frost is its own, but fire is its enemy.
hraesvelg_eagle.source: Vafthrudnismal 37; Snorri, Gylfaginning 18 (Hraesvelgr at heaven's end).

rime_thurs.lore: The line of Ymir grew out of the rime, and the fire of Muspell melted the ice from which they came.
rime_thurs.source: Snorri, Gylfaginning 5 (Ymir from the rime of Elivagar where it met Muspell's heat).

kallikantzaros.lore: The goblins of Christmas fear fire, so the hearth is kept burning for all twelve nights, until the blessing of the waters at Epiphany sends them back below.
kallikantzaros.source: Greek and Balkan folklore of the kallikantzaroi (the Yule log kept burning; the Epiphany blessing).

mushmahhu.lore: Tiamat filled her monsters with venom in place of blood, and so poison cannot hurt what is its own blood.
mushmahhu.source: Enuma Elish, tablet I (the eleven monsters, 'venom for blood').

kyubi_kitsune.lore: The fox's fire is her own and cannot burn her, but a mirror held up by the court diviner showed what she was.
kyubi_kitsune.source: The legend of Tamamo-no-Mae (Otogizoshi; the Noh play Sessho-seki).

viy.lore: The chief of the gnomes is caked with earth and has a face of iron: blades scrape off him, yet the danger is his gaze and not his hide.
viy.source: Gogol, Viy (1835), with his own note on the folk figure.

image_of_the_beast.lore: This idol was cast in gold, so that blades skate off the metal, but a hammer will break it.
image_of_the_beast.source: Revelation 13:14-15 (the image given breath to speak).

polyphemus.lore: Odysseus made the Cyclops drunk with strong wine, and while he slept drove a stake of olive wood into his one eye, for he is beaten by wine and by blinding, and by the point of a stake rather than a club.
polyphemus.source: Homer, Odyssey 9 (the wine of Maron, the stake cut from the giant's own olive-wood club).

mandrake.lore: A root has no mind to be frightened or charmed and it never sleeps, and its sap, which brings slumber to others, is no poison to itself.
mandrake.source: Theophrastus, Historia Plantarum 9.8; Dioscorides on the root boiled in wine.

kappa.lore: When a kappa is knocked senseless the water spills from its dish, and so a stun is its undoing.

eloko.lore: The biloko are spirits of the forest, and no sleep comes to them.

asanbosam.lore: It dwells in the high branches and has teeth of iron, and no charm can turn it.
asanbosam.source: Akan folklore; Edward Long, The History of Jamaica (1774).

ahuizotl.lore: The beast of the lake cries like a child and has a hand upon its tail, yet it is flesh and blood and nothing stranger.

khalkotauros.lore: The bronze bulls of Hephaestus breathe fire and cannot burn, and a blade glances from their plates, but a hammer dents them.

cu_sith.lore: The hound of the fairies never sleeps upon the hunt, and no charm can turn it aside.
cu_sith.source: J. G. Campbell, Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900).

bulgasari.lore: This beast was grown from rice and iron, and a blade that sinks into the metal of its hide is eaten, but a hammer bruises it still.
bulgasari.source: Jo Jae-sam, Songnam Japji; the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture.

vetala.lore: A spirit that wears a dead body knows neither fear nor sleep nor poison.

nahual.lore: Beneath the skin he is a man, and whatever frightens men frightens him.

likho.lore: Likho has but one eye, and if you put it out, as the smith did, she is helpless.

centaur.lore: The horse-men are wild and fearless in battle, but wine sends them reeling, and when they drank it at the wedding of the Lapiths the fight began.

blue_men_of_the_minch.lore: The sea-men of the fair folk raise up the gales, and sleep never takes them.

vila.lore: A fairy of the clouds can be neither lulled to sleep nor charmed.

myrmekes.lore: These ants of the desert dig all day, but a cold night slows them and a hammer cracks their shells.

ponaturi.lore: They are a people of the dark beneath the sea, and they are dazzled by the light that slew them in the tale of Tawhaki.

taniwha.lore: The water-dragon has scales that turn a thrust, and no sleep comes to such a guardian.
taniwha.source: Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand: 'Taniwha'.

impundulu.lore: Neither spear nor gun can harm the lightning bird, nor can it be poisoned, but fire destroys it.
impundulu.source: Axel-Ivar Berglund, Zulu Thought-Patterns and Symbolism (1975).

mapinguari.lore: Arrows and knives are turned by its hide everywhere save at the navel, and its own stench troubles it not at all.

preta.lore: The hungry ghost has no sleep and no blood for poison, and nothing but food will charm it.

upas_tree.lore: A tree that poisons the very air is proof against poison, and being a tree it neither fears nor sleeps.
upas_tree.source: Erasmus Darwin, The Loves of the Plants (1789).

nuckelavee.lore: The demon of the Orkney shore fears nothing in the world but fresh water.
nuckelavee.source: Walter Traill Dennison, The Scottish Antiquary (1891).

star_jelly.lore: The trembling jelly has no eyes and no mind, nor any blood.

psoglav.lore: Its single eye sees so poorly that to blind it avails nothing.

waq_waq_tree.lore: This tree bears heads that cry, yet it does not sleep or fear or see as we do.
waq_waq_tree.source: The Arabic and Persian wonder-books; al-Qazwini, 'Aja'ib al-makhluqat.

yuki_onna.lore: The snow woman cannot be frozen and her blizzard never sleeps, and a blade passes through her as through snow.

yacumama.lore: The mother of the waters lies in her pool and never sleeps.

tsuchigumo.lore: Its swollen and hairy body cares nothing for a club, and it was a sword that cut it down.
tsuchigumo.source: The Heike Monogatari, Tsurugi no maki.

bhuta_vahana_yanta.lore: Spirits drive these engines of bronze and wood, which have no mind, no blood, no sleep and no eyes to blind.

reem.lore: The wild ox as big as a hill has no fear of anything that walks.

eitr.lore: The first poison of the world can be neither poisoned nor frozen.

bakunawa.lore: The serpent that swallows moons cannot be blinded by any light.

grick.lore: The grick's rubbery hide gives under blade and point like wet leather, though magic will search it through.
grick.source: Dungeons & Dragons, Monster Manual (2014): the grick resists ordinary weapons. Of those, the club is left to the hero (ruling B3).
